learning_outcomes: Explain aI Myths, Misconceptions, and Terminology and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study aI Myths, Misconceptions, and Terminology within History, Categories, and Approaches to AI. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: AI contains multiple traditions and capability labels. Compare systems by what they do, how they work, and the evidence available—not by hype.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Plausible language and high confidence-like scores do not guarantee factual correctness. Correlation is not causation, and a model’s observed behavior is not evidence on its own of consciousness or general intelligence.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: AI versus ordinary automation
items.text: Automation follows a defined workflow; AI may add learned predictions, perception, ranking, or generated candidates. Compare the AI approach with a simpler rule-based or manual baseline before adding complexity.

items.title: Data correlation versus causation
items.text: Correlation measures association, not necessarily a causal relationship. Confounders, selection effects, or shared trends may explain the relationship, so causal claims need a suitable design and evidence.

items.title: Why a fluent response does not establish factual accuracy
items.text: Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. It can be misleading when one class dominates or errors have different consequences; compare with additional task-specific metrics.

items.title: What model confidence does and does not mean
items.text: What model confidence does and does not mean is one of the concepts used to reason about ai myths, misconceptions, and terminology. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what ai myths, misconceptions, and terminology takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. AI contains multiple traditions and capability labels. Compare systems by what they do, how they work, and the evidence available—not by hype.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Plausible language and high confidence-like scores do not guarantee factual correctness. Correlation is not causation, and a model’s observed behavior is not evidence on its own of consciousness or general intelligence. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: take five example systems related to ai myths, misconceptions, and terminology. Classify each by its task, input, output, and AI approach; justify one ambiguous case and state evidence that would change your classification.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
